Avogadro guide · Minecraft 1.12.2 / Cleanroom

Chains, networks, and crystals

Build a chain from repeated fragments, join chains with branches or crosslinks, or repeat a crystal cell. Start with the PEG chain below: supply its repeat unit, its length, and both end groups to get a finite model with a known formula.

Calls used in the examples

Calls used in this guide
Call or setting Arguments What it does
attachment(name, index) Attachment name; atom index Name the atoms used to connect repeat units or end groups.
PolymerDefinition.usingAttachments(...) Unit; connection names; displacement; bond type; end groups Describe how supplied pieces join; the complete example gives their ordering.
Vector(x, y, z) Repeat displacement Place the next copy relative to the previous copy.

When you finish: A builder creates a model but does not add it to the game. Java registrations use a name, called an owner, to group the definitions your mod controls; choose your mod ID. A RegistrationJob lets you cancel pending work or remove its installed set later. JSON and Groovy registrations use their file or script loading rules instead. Keep drawing and exports in client code. The builder does not invent missing hydrogens or end groups; supply them when your finite model needs them.

Make a PEG chain with real end groups

The PEG recipe repeats a supplied ethylene-glycol fragment and adds the atoms at both ends. A count of four produces the finite molecule shown below. The end groups are supplied explicitly; the builder does not guess them.

Java · add this method to your class.

public static PolymerDefinition peg() {
    // HO–(CH2–CH2–O)n–H. Caps supply both terminal hydrogens and the extra oxygen.
    var unit = new StructureBuilder().atom("C", 0, 0, 0)
            .atom("C", 1.5, 0, 0).atom("O", 2.9, .2, 0)
            .atom("H", -.3, .8, .65).atom("H", -.3, -.8, -.65)
            .atom("H", 1.7, .8, -.65).atom("H", 1.7, -.8, .65)
            .bond(0, 1).bond(1, 2).bond(0, 3).bond(0, 4).bond(1, 5).bond(1, 6)
            .attachment("head", 0).attachment("tail", 2).build();
    var head = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", -1.4, -.2, 0)
            .atom("H", -2.2, .2, 0).bond(0, 1).attachment("end", 0).build();
    var tail = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", 3.8, .2, 0).attachment("end", 0).build();
    return PolymerDefinition.usingAttachments(unit, "head", "tail",
            new PolymerDefinition.Vector(4.3, 0, 0), BondType.SINGLE,
            PolymerDefinition.Cap.usingAttachment(head, "end", BondType.SINGLE),
            PolymerDefinition.Cap.usingAttachment(tail, "end", BondType.SINGLE), 4);
}

import io.github.wurtzitane.avogadro.api.*

def molecules = mods.avogadro.molecules
def molecule = molecules.builder("guide:peg")
molecule.name("Polyethylene glycol")
molecule.classification(MoleculeClassification.POLYMER)
def fragment1 = molecules.structureBuilder()
fragment1.atom("C", 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
fragment1.atom("C", 1.5, 0.0, 0.0)
fragment1.atom("O", 2.9, 0.2, 0.0)
fragment1.atom("H", -0.3, 0.8, 0.65)
fragment1.atom("H", -0.3, -0.8, -0.65)
fragment1.atom("H", 1.7, 0.8, -0.65)
fragment1.atom("H", 1.7, -0.8, 0.65)
fragment1.bond(0, 1, BondType.SINGLE)
fragment1.bond(1, 2, BondType.SINGLE)
fragment1.bond(0, 3, BondType.SINGLE)
fragment1.bond(0, 4, BondType.SINGLE)
fragment1.bond(1, 5, BondType.SINGLE)
fragment1.bond(1, 6, BondType.SINGLE)
fragment1.attachment("head", 0)
fragment1.attachment("tail", 2)
def geometry2 = fragment1.build()
def fragment3 = molecules.structureBuilder()
fragment3.atom("O", -1.4, -0.2, 0.0)
fragment3.atom("H", -2.2, 0.2, 0.0)
fragment3.bond(0, 1, BondType.SINGLE)
fragment3.attachment("end", 0)
def geometry4 = fragment3.build()
def fragment5 = molecules.structureBuilder()
fragment5.atom("H", 3.8, 0.2, 0.0)
fragment5.attachment("end", 0)
def geometry6 = fragment5.build()
molecule.polymer(new PolymerDefinition(geometry2, 0, 2, new PolymerDefinition.Vector(4.3, 0.0, 0.0), BondType.SINGLE, new PolymerDefinition.Cap(geometry4, 0, BondType.SINGLE), new PolymerDefinition.Cap(geometry6, 0, BondType.SINGLE), 4))
molecules.register(molecule)

Expected result At n = 4: C8H18O5, 31 atoms. The end groups matter: repeating C2H4O alone would miss H2O.

What a polymer network looks like

In this idealized model, two 1,4-polyisoprene chains can be joined by single sulfur bridges. Each eligible position explicitly chooses either one shared sulfur atom or two separate H caps. The model does not remove hydrogens implicitly and does not simulate vulcanization, stereochemistry, elasticity, or chemical stability.

Java · add this method to your class.

public static StructureFragment rubberUnit() {
    // 1,4-polyisoprene repeat with one deliberately open site at C4.
    // A separate choice supplies either H or a shared sulfur bridge there.
    return new StructureBuilder()
            .atom("C", 0, 0, 0).atom("C", 1.5, 0, 0)
            .atom("C", 2.8, .4, 0).atom("C", 4.2, .4, 0).atom("C", 1.5, -1.5, 0)
            .atom("H", -.4, .7, .7).atom("H", -.4, .7, -.7)
            .atom("H", 2.9, 1.4, 0).atom("H", 4.4, .4, 1)
            .atom("H", .5, -1.9, 0).atom("H", 2, -1.9, .8).atom("H", 2, -1.9, -.8)
            .bond(0, 1).bond(1, 2, BondType.DOUBLE).bond(2, 3).bond(1, 4)
            .bond(0, 5).bond(0, 6).bond(2, 7).bond(3, 8)
            .bond(4, 9).bond(4, 10).bond(4, 11)
            .attachment("head", 0).attachment("tail", 3).attachment("cross", 3).build();
}

This operation runs in code. JSON stores definitions and recipes; it cannot call this method or handle events. Select or for the working example.

Java · add this method to your class.

public static PolymerNetworkDefinition rubber() {
    var sulfur = new StructureBuilder().atom("S", 4.2, 2.2, 0)
            .attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 0).build();
    var hydrogens = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", 4.2, 1.4, 0)
            .atom("H", 4.2, 3.0, 0).attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 1).build();
    var pair = StructureAssembly.builder()
            .part("left", rubberUnit()).part("right", rubberUnit().translate(0, 3.6, 0))
            .choice("bridge", "sulfur_bridge", "bridgeChance",
                    StructureAssembly.builder().part("connector", sulfur).build(),
                    StructureAssembly.builder().part("connector", hydrogens).build())
            .link("left/cross", "bridge/connector/left", BondType.SINGLE)
            .link("right/cross", "bridge/connector/right", BondType.SINGLE).build();
    var head = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", -1, 0, 0).atom("H", -1, 3.6, 0)
            .attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 1).build();
    var tail = new StructureBuilder().atom("H", 5.2, .4, 0).atom("H", 5.2, 4, 0)
            .attachment("left", 0).attachment("right", 1).build();
    var assembly = StructureAssembly.builder()
            .repeat("pairs", pair, "length", StructureAssembly.translation(5.7, 0, 0))
            .neighbor("left/tail", "left/head", 1, BondType.SINGLE)
            .neighbor("right/tail", "right/head", 1, BondType.SINGLE)
            .endGroups(StructureAssembly.builder().part("cap", head).build(),
                    StructureAssembly.builder().part("cap", tail).build())
            .link("pairs/head/cap/left", "pairs[first]/left/head", BondType.SINGLE)
            .link("pairs/head/cap/right", "pairs[first]/right/head", BondType.SINGLE)
            .link("pairs[last]/left/tail", "pairs/tail/cap/left", BondType.SINGLE)
            .link("pairs[last]/right/tail", "pairs/tail/cap/right", BondType.SINGLE).build();
    return new PolymerNetworkDefinition(List.of(
            PolymerNetworkDefinition.Parameter.count("length", 1, 16, 4),
            PolymerNetworkDefinition.Parameter.probability("bridgeChance", .5)), assembly, 42L);
}

public static PolymerPreview realization(int length, double chance, long seed) {
    // Seed controls the choices, not the authored atom positions.
    return rubber().preview(new NetworkPreviewRequest(
            Map.of("length", length), Map.of("bridgeChance", chance), seed));
}

Expected result For length n and k selected sulfur bridges: C(10n)H(16n+4−2k)S(k), omitting S when k = 0. Each C has total bond order 4, H has 1, and bridging S has 2.
Tip Changing the seed changes which eligible occurrences are selected. It does not randomize coordinates or produce a relaxed polymer conformation. Keep rule IDs and instance names stable if you want stable seeded results.

Choose connection points in repeated fragments

Choose connection points in repeated fragments
Path / setting Meaning
pairs[0]/left/head Head atom of the first left repeat
pairs[first] / pairs[last] First / last repeat without hard-coding the count
pairs[*]/left/cross All matching left-side sites in stable instance order
Equal-length endpoint selections Pair corresponding endpoints
One endpoint and several endpoints Broadcast the single endpoint
Other unequal lengths Validation failure; no silent zip/truncation
neighbor(from, to, offset, type) Repeat-relative links; skip links crossing an open boundary
Parent → node → repeat-step → body Order in which authored transforms apply
End-group coordinates Relative to the first / last repeat frame
Nested repeats/groups Use the same rules for a backbone, branch, or finite repeated motif
Choose connection points in repeated fragments
JSON path / field Meaning
pairs[0]/left/head Head atom of the first left repeat; use attachment paths in from/to fields.
pairs[first] / pairs[last] First / last repeat without hard-coding its count.
pairs[*]/left/cross All matching left-side sites in stable instance order.
links[].from / links[].to Equal-length selections pair corresponding atoms. A singleton broadcasts; other unequal lengths fail.
Repeat node neighbor_links[] Each entry has from, to, offset, and type. Links crossing an open repeat boundary are skipped.
Node transform, repeat step, and body Transforms apply in parent → node → repeat-step → body order.
Repeat node head / tail End-group assemblies use the first / last repeat frame.
Nested body.nodes[] The same rules work for backbones, branches, and finite motifs.

Add random bonds without exceeding each atom’s limit

Choices can replace a complete branch with an explicit absent alternative. Random links instead sample an authored pool of endpoint pairs. The small real-species example below joins two hydroxyl radicals into hydrogen peroxide at probability 1; lower probabilities intentionally leave reactive radicals. It is not an example of finished water.

Java · add this method to your class.

public static PolymerNetworkDefinition reactiveSites() {
    // Two authored hydroxyl radicals. At p=1 they form H–O–O–H.
    // At p=0 they remain radicals, not two water molecules.
    var left = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", -.7, 0, 0).atom("H", -1.1, .85, 0)
            .bond(0, 1).attachment("site", 0).attachment("alias", 0).randomLinkCapacity(0, 1).build();
    var right = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", .7, 0, 0).atom("H", 1.1, -.85, 0)
            .bond(0, 1).attachment("site", 0).randomLinkCapacity(0, 1).build();
    var assembly = StructureAssembly.builder().part("left", left).part("right", right)
            .randomLinks("peroxide_bond", "left/site", "right/site", "paired", "chance", BondType.SINGLE)
            .build();
    return new PolymerNetworkDefinition(List.of(
            PolymerNetworkDefinition.Parameter.probability("chance", 1)), assembly, 42L);
}

Groovy · same API; place methods in your script or client helper as described. 

static PolymerNetworkDefinition reactiveSites() {
    // Two authored hydroxyl radicals. At p=1 they form H–O–O–H.
    // At p=0 they remain radicals, not two water molecules.
    def left = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", -.7, 0, 0).atom("H", -1.1, .85, 0)
            .bond(0, 1).attachment("site", 0).attachment("alias", 0).randomLinkCapacity(0, 1).build();
    def right = new StructureBuilder().atom("O", .7, 0, 0).atom("H", 1.1, -.85, 0)
            .bond(0, 1).attachment("site", 0).randomLinkCapacity(0, 1).build();
    def assembly = StructureAssembly.builder().part("left", left).part("right", right)
            .randomLinks("peroxide_bond", "left/site", "right/site", "paired", "chance", BondType.SINGLE)
            .build();
    return new PolymerNetworkDefinition(List.of(
            PolymerNetworkDefinition.Parameter.probability("chance", 1)), assembly, 42L);
}

Add random bonds without exceeding each atom’s limit
Pool / rule Behavior
paired Corresponding endpoints; equal selection lengths required
broadcast One endpoint against a selection
cartesian Every authored endpoint on one side against every endpoint on the other
randomLinkCapacity(atom, count) Additional random links allowed at that atom; attachment aliases share the same capacity
Probability then capacity Sample candidates by chance, process passing candidates in seeded order, reject those exceeding capacity
Diagnostics Read actual branch/link counts and capacity exclusions from preview.diagnostics()
Density A chance is not a guarantee of an exact final link count
Reproduction Versioned SHA-256 sampling of seed, rule ID, phase, and stable instance paths; version 1; 64-bit seed stored as a decimal string
Add random bonds without exceeding each atom’s limit
JSON field / value Behavior
random_links[].pairing: "paired" Corresponding endpoints; selections must have equal lengths.
pairing: "broadcast" One endpoint against a selection.
pairing: "cartesian" Every selected endpoint on one side against every selected endpoint on the other.
Fragment random_link_capacities An object mapping local atom indices to additional-link capacities. Attachment aliases share their atom’s capacity.
probability A number from 0 to 1 or a declared probability parameter name. Passing candidates are processed in seeded order, subject to capacities.
Result counters These are calculated when the recipe expands, not authored JSON fields. Runtime code can read them through PolymerPreview.
random_version: 1 and seed: "42" Store the signed 64-bit seed as a decimal string. Keep rule IDs and instance paths stable for reproducible choices.

The polymer examiner exposes counts, probabilities, seed entry, next seed, and reset. Changes stay in that viewing session. It keeps camera/pause state and the last successful model while the next one prepares; a failed or superseded request must not replace a valid preview. Formula and mass stay below the model. The sidebar contains only its settings. Integrations can read atom/bond and random-pattern counts from the successful PolymerPreview; the viewer does not list internal expansion counters.

Export that PolymerPreview, rather than rebuilding defaults: see exact network exports. A saved sidecar retains the parameters, algorithm version, and seed. Template-local atomic overrides repeat with each instance. Flattened network-wide atom overrides are rejected because indices change with counts.

Translate control labels. Set a parameter’s label to a language key and add that key to your language file. Literal labels work too. Unlabeled length and bridgeChance controls use Avogadro’s “Chain length” and “Bridge chance” entries. Changing a display label keeps the parameter identifier and saved settings intact.

Network limits

Network limits
Limit Maximum / rule
Expanded atoms / bonds 4,096 / 8,192
Declared parameters 8 total
One repeat count 1–64, also within its parameter bounds
Template nodes / nesting 64 / 16
Candidate endpoint pairs 65,536 per preview
Defaults Must build a valid preview
An oversized requested realization Rejected; never truncated or reseeded

Repeat a sodium chloride cell

Java · add this method to your class.

public static StructureFragment saltBasis() {
    // Conventional rock-salt cell, a = 5.64 Å. No covalent Na–Cl bonds.
    var basis = new StructureBuilder();
    double a = 5.64;
    double[][] sodium = {{0,0,0}, {0,.5,.5}, {.5,0,.5}, {.5,.5,0}};
    double[][] chlorine = {{.5,.5,.5}, {.5,0,0}, {0,.5,0}, {0,0,.5}};
    for (double[] p : sodium) {
        int atom = basis.addAtom("Na", p[0]*a, p[1]*a, p[2]*a);
        basis.atomConfiguration(atom, new AtomicConfiguration(11, 12, 1, List.of(2,8)));
    }
    for (double[] p : chlorine) {
        int atom = basis.addAtom("Cl", p[0]*a, p[1]*a, p[2]*a);
        basis.atomConfiguration(atom, new AtomicConfiguration(17, 18, -1, List.of(2,8,8)));
    }
    return basis.build();
}

import io.github.wurtzitane.avogadro.api.*

def molecules = mods.avogadro.molecules
def molecule = molecules.builder("guide:salt")
molecule.name("Sodium chloride")
molecule.formula("NaCl")
def fragment1 = molecules.structureBuilder()
fragment1.atom("Na", 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(0, new AtomicConfiguration(11, 12, 1, java.util.List.of(2, 8)))
fragment1.atom("Na", 0.0, 2.82, 2.82)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(1, new AtomicConfiguration(11, 12, 1, java.util.List.of(2, 8)))
fragment1.atom("Na", 2.82, 0.0, 2.82)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(2, new AtomicConfiguration(11, 12, 1, java.util.List.of(2, 8)))
fragment1.atom("Na", 2.82, 2.82, 0.0)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(3, new AtomicConfiguration(11, 12, 1, java.util.List.of(2, 8)))
fragment1.atom("Cl", 2.82, 2.82, 2.82)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(4, new AtomicConfiguration(17, 18, -1, java.util.List.of(2, 8, 8)))
fragment1.atom("Cl", 2.82, 0.0, 0.0)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(5, new AtomicConfiguration(17, 18, -1, java.util.List.of(2, 8, 8)))
fragment1.atom("Cl", 0.0, 2.82, 0.0)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(6, new AtomicConfiguration(17, 18, -1, java.util.List.of(2, 8, 8)))
fragment1.atom("Cl", 0.0, 0.0, 2.82)
fragment1.atomConfiguration(7, new AtomicConfiguration(17, 18, -1, java.util.List.of(2, 8, 8)))
def geometry2 = fragment1.build()
molecule.structure(geometry2)
molecule.classification(MoleculeClassification.CRYSTAL)
molecule.crystalCell(new CrystalCell(5.64, 5.64, 5.64, 90.0, 90.0, 90.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0))
molecules.register(molecule)

The conventional cell contains four Na and four Cl positions; its composition reduces to NaCl. crystalCell stores cell dimensions and angles. CrystalGeometry.repeat makes a finite viewing cluster.

Java · add this method to your class.

public static MoleculeStructure saltCube() {
    // 3 cells on each axis: 27 conventional cells, 216 ions.
    return CrystalGeometry.repeat(saltBasis().toStructure("guide:salt_basis"),
            new CrystalCell(5.64, 5.64, 5.64, 90, 90, 90), 3, false);
}

public static StructureFragment saltBasis() {
    // Conventional rock-salt cell, a = 5.64 Å. No covalent Na–Cl bonds.
    var basis = new StructureBuilder();
    double a = 5.64;
    double[][] sodium = {{0, 0, 0}, {0, .5, .5}, {.5, 0, .5}, {.5, .5, 0}};
    double[][] chlorine = {{.5, .5, .5}, {.5, 0, 0}, {0, .5, 0}, {0, 0, .5}};
    for (double[] p : sodium) {
        int atom = basis.addAtom("Na", p[0] * a, p[1] * a, p[2] * a);
        basis.atomConfiguration(atom, new AtomicConfiguration(11, 12, 1, List.of(2, 8)));
    }
    for (double[] p : chlorine) {
        int atom = basis.addAtom("Cl", p[0] * a, p[1] * a, p[2] * a);
        basis.atomConfiguration(atom, new AtomicConfiguration(17, 18, -1, List.of(2, 8, 8)));
    }
    return basis.build();
}

Expected result 3 × 3 × 3 conventional cells: 108 Na and 108 Cl, 216 atoms total. No ordinary covalent bonds are drawn between ions.
Tip For lower-level periodic fragments use cell(vectors), link(from,to,offset,type), and repeat(counts,wrap). Cell links must be authored chemical bonds when you intend to draw bonds; ionic neighbors are not automatically covalent connections. wrapCylinder wraps an authored periodic sheet; it does not optimize a nanotube.

References for these models

ICSC: PEG formula · IUPAC: vulcanization and sulfide crosslinks · TU Graz: rock-salt cell positions.

Keep adjusted previews when rebuilding

Root constraints and atom annotation overrides are retained with a template. MoleculeEdits.preparePreview(definition, geometry) reapplies them to the selected finite expansion. Indices refer to that selected atom order; incompatible targets reject the new request while the examiner retains its previous successful geometry. A template preview must preserve its recipe’s indexed element and bond graph. Materialize the preview before changing topology.

preview.withPostprocessing(definition) retains parameters, seed, atomic configurations and attachment points, and adds the adjusted finite realized_structure to export reproduction data. Fragment annotations survive linear-chain and crystal repetition. Exact attachment paths use direct lookup; wildcard matching has a two-million-comparison budget and exposes selector_comparisons diagnostics.

Network previews with a chance below 100% omit formula and mass labels. Probability controls are hidden when their authored default is 100%. Counts and the exact generated geometry remain available.

A crystal box follows the authored cell origin and lattice vectors. A finite basis uses one representative of each periodic atom, so its visible cluster can sit off-center inside the box. Rock salt is one example; the box is not recentered on the cluster.
